name: Al Shouf Cedar Nature Reserve
blurb: Ancient cedars, oak slopes and a rewilding ibex herd in Mount Lebanon.

tip.title: Thin the snowpack
tip.text: Cedar and juniper stands rely on winter snow. Cut Winter snow by 80% and watch the trees, then the browsers and predators that depend on them.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Al Shouf Cedar Nature Reserve

notes: The species list comes from GBIF occurrence records inside a circle around the park, so it can include nearby areas. Feeding links come from GloBI records and the sources listed where they state them; others are general ecology and are illustrative.

nodes.name: Wild grasses
nodes.desc: Wild goatgrasses and other annual herbs of open slopes and clearings, grazed by wild and domestic hoofed animals.
Omnivore that digs for roots and bulbs and eats acorns. Wolves are its main predator across much of its range.
A small gazelle listed among the reserve's mammals and a recorded prey of red fox.
Extinct in Lebanon since the mid-19th century; a herd from Jordan was brought to the reserve in 2017. It eats grasses and leaves and stays near cliffs for safety.

nodes.name: Cape hyrax
nodes.desc: A rock-dwelling herbivore recorded near the reserve.
Browsing by goats on young cedars hinders regeneration of the forest. Jackals and wolves take livestock.
Small omnivorous rodent eaten by jackals, foxes, hedgehogs and snakes in recorded GloBI interactions.
Opportunistic omnivore that eats rodents, birds, reptiles and fruit, and scavenges carcasses. Wolves dominate it.
Generalist hunter and scavenger; GloBI records it eating gazelle, mice, hedgehogs and snakes among these species.
Small ground forager; GloBI records it eating mice and snakes.
Eats mostly snakes, plus some lizards. Populations in the Middle East are resident.
Raptor listed among the reserve's birds. It feeds on carcasses of large animals.
Listed among the reserve's mammals. Wolves are the main predator of wild boar and dominate jackals.
A large eagle listed among the reserve's raptors; it is a recorded predator of Nubian ibex.
Heavy snow cover blankets the high cedar slopes and melts into water for spring growth.
Mediterranean winter rains water the oaks and grasses.
Fungi, bacteria and invertebrates recycling dead wood, leaves and carcasses.

story: Al Shouf Cedar Nature Reserve is a forest located in the Chouf and Aley districts of Lebanon on the slopes of Jebel Baruk mountain. Covering 550 km2, it is the largest natural reserve in Lebanon. It contains the Lebanon cedar forests of Barouk, Maaser el Shouf and Ain Zhalta-Bmohray.
matters: The reserve forms the last natural limits to the spread of Cedrus libani on the planet. Its forests play a crucial role as a carbon sink and help stabilize and protect soils on steep slopes.
